\chapter{In the House}
\label{ch:ka-house}
\hlchaptermodality{56}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five ordinary things in a Kannada house, and say which two of them arrived with borrowed names.}

Complete KA-C56-box and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cāpe]{\kn{ಚಾಪೆ} (cāpe) — a mat}

\label{lesson:KA-C56-mat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{haḷḷi} mean, and what did \emph{dāri} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಚಾಪೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಚಾಪೆ}} (\emph{cāpe}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mat\textquotedblright{}.

The woven mat that gets unrolled on the floor: for sitting on, for eating on, for sleeping on, and for putting away against the wall in the morning.

The \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ} arrived from outside with its Persian name, and it arrived late. The \kn{ಚಾಪೆ} was already there. A Kannada house has for a very long time sat and eaten and slept at floor level, and the \kn{ಚಾಪೆ} is the piece of furniture that arrangement needs — one object doing what a chair, a table and a bed do elsewhere, then rolling up to occupy nothing.

Offering a guest a \kn{ಚಾಪೆ} is the older form of the courtesy the \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ} now performs, and in a \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ} it is still the usual one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a Kannada house keeps to hand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cāpe}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kuḷitukō}, then \emph{cāpe}, and say who is offered which
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಚಾಪೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[buṭṭi]{\kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} (buṭṭi) — a basket}

\label{lesson:KA-C56-basket}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cāpe} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ}} (\emph{buṭṭi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a basket\textquotedblright{}.

Woven, usually from bamboo, and carried on the hip or the head rather than in the hand. \kn{ಹಣ್ಣಿನ} \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} is a basket of fruit; a \kn{ಹೂವಿನ} \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} is what flowers come to the door in.

The little \emph{-ina} in the middle of those is the joining piece Kannada slips between two names to say the second belongs to the first. Fruit-of basket. You can build the same shape with anything you already have.

\kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} shares its ending with the \kn{ಚಾಪೆ}'s world rather than the \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ}'s: another light, cheap, repairable thing made from what grows nearby, and one that a house replaces every few years without thinking about it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a thing to sit on, and a thing to carry with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{buṭṭi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{haṇṇina buṭṭi}, then \emph{hūvina buṭṭi}, and hear the joining piece in the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a basket\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cāku]{\kn{ಚಾಕು} (cāku) — a knife}

\label{lesson:KA-C56-knife}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{buṭṭi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಚಾಕು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಚಾಕು}} (\emph{cāku}) — \textquotedblleft{}a knife\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{chāqū}, a small knife, carried down into the subcontinent along the same road that delivered the \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ}, and handed on to Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and this. Two objects in two chapters, both borrowed, both arriving by the north.

The borrowing did not push anything out. Kannada's own blade is \kn{ಕತ್ತಿ} (\emph{katti}), and it is the big one — the household and field blade, the one a \kn{ರೈತ} works with. \kn{ಚಾಕು} is the small one: the pocket knife, the paring knife, the thing that cuts a \kn{ಹಣ್ಣು}.

The pattern is the one the chair showed. When a language borrows a word for a thing it already has, the borrowed word usually takes a narrower job and the old word keeps the wider one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the second of them arrived by the northern road.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cāku}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kurci}, then \emph{cāku}, and say what the two of them have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಚಾಕು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a knife\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pātre]{\kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ} (pātre) — a vessel, a cooking pot}

\label{lesson:KA-C56-vessel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cāku} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ}} (\emph{pātre}) — \textquotedblleft{}a vessel, a cooking pot\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{pātra}, and it began by meaning a drinking or eating vessel. Then it did something quietly remarkable: it moved from the container to the person. A \emph{pātra} is also one fit to receive — a worthy recipient of a gift, of teaching, of trust.

From there it took one more step, and the \emph{pātra} of a play is a character, a part, a role. The same word holds the pot, the deserving person and the actor's part, because all three are shapes that something is poured into.

Kannada carries the whole set. \kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ} in the kitchen is the vessel; \kn{ಪಾತ್ರ} on the stage is the role. One Sanskrit word, and the ending tells you which of its lives is being lived.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one keeps three meanings in one shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pātre}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pātre}, then \emph{nīru}, and say which one holds the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a vessel, a cooking pot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[peṭṭige]{\kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ} (peṭṭige) — a box}

\label{lesson:KA-C56-box}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pātre} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ}} (\emph{peṭṭige}) — \textquotedblleft{}a box\textquotedblright{}.

All four sisters have this word and it is nearly the same in each: Tamil \emph{peṭṭi}, Malayalam \emph{peṭṭi}, Telugu \emph{peṭṭe}, and Kannada \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ}. Only Kannada carries the extra closing syllable, which is a habit you have now seen a few times — Kannada tends to be the long one.

A \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ} is the wooden or tin chest a household keeps its papers and its good \kn{ಬಟ್ಟೆ} in, standing in a corner with a padlock on it. It is also the word that stretched to cover a suitcase, a jewellery box and the case a musical instrument travels in.

Notice how much of this chapter is containers. The \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ} carries, the \kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ} cooks, the \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ} keeps. A house is largely a set of things for putting other things into.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಚಾಪೆ}, \kn{ಬುಟ್ಟಿ}, \kn{ಚಾಕು}, \kn{ಪಾತ್ರೆ}, \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ}. You can furnish a room.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{peṭṭige}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say which three of them hold something
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a box\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
